subject: Efficiently constraining parameters for identification in a latent variable model

messages.author: 0001c090d17a225a
messages.subject: Efficiently constraining parameters for identification in a latent variable model
parts:
Dear List,

I have implemented Hoff, Raftery & Handcock's (JASA 2002) latent space model for social networks in Stan. I believe everything is more or less working, though I had a question on the efficiency of my method of guaranteeing identification of the model (model below; full replication code for a Poisson version is attached). 

For a 2-dimensional latent space model, I constrain the latent positions of the first three observations in the parameters{} block to lie in particular quadrants in R^2. In the model{} block, the latent positions of these observations also get their own priors before they are merged with the rest of the observations to form a n-by-2 matrix of latent positions (from which pairwise Euclidean distances are calculated). 

Is this the proper/efficient way to go about constraining particular elements of a matrix in Stan? Beyond fixing the observations' positions (my solution in a previous maximum likelihood version), any other ideas on how I can help guarantee identification? I am new to Bayesian modeling and Stan, so any suggestions would be welcomed.

Regards,
~Jason

space_model <- '
data {
    int<lower=1> n;            // number of nodes
    int<lower=1> N;            // number of dyads
    int<lower=1> K;            // number of dimensions in latent space
    int<lower=0> y[N];         // outcome
}
parameters {
    real beta;

    // constrain the latent positions of the first three observations to help
    // ensure identification.
    real<lower=-5,upper=0> pos_x1;
    real<lower=-5,upper=0> pos_y1;

    real<lower=0,upper=5> pos_x2;
    real<lower=0,upper=5> pos_y2;

    real<lower=-5,upper=0> pos_x3;
    real<lower=0,upper=5> pos_y3;

    matrix<lower=-10,upper=10>[n-3,K] pos_raw;
}
model {
    matrix[n,K] pos;               // positions with constrained obs added
    vector[N] D;                   // container for pairwise distances
    int idx;                       // counter

    // construct positions matrix
    pos[1,1] <- pos_x1;
    pos[1,2] <- pos_y1;
    pos[2,1] <- pos_x2;
    pos[2,2] <- pos_y2;
    pos[3,1] <- pos_x3;
    pos[3,2] <- pos_y3;

    for (i in 1:(n-3)) {
        pos[i+3,1] <- pos_raw[i,1];
        pos[i+3,2] <- pos_raw[i,2];
    }

    // priors
    beta ~ normal(0, 10);

    pos_x1 ~ normal(-2.5, 2);
    pos_y1 ~ normal(-2.5, 2);
    pos_x2 ~ normal( 2.5, 2);
    pos_y2 ~ normal( 2.5, 2);
    pos_x3 ~ normal(-2.5, 2);
    pos_y3 ~ normal( 2.5, 2);

    pos_raw[n-3,K] ~ normal(0, 4);

    // calculate pairwise distances
    idx <- 1;
    for (i in 1:(n-1)) {
        for (j in (i+1):n) {
            D[idx] <- sqrt(dot_self(pos[i] - pos[j]));
            idx <- idx+1;
        }
    }

    y ~ poisson(exp(beta - D));
}
'

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Efficiently constraining parameters for identification in a latent variable model
parts:
On 9/8/13 4:16 PM, Jason Morgan wrote:
> Dear List,
>
> I have implemented Hoff, Raftery & Handcock's (JASA 2002) latent space model for social networks in Stan. I believe
> everything is more or less working, though I had a question on the efficiency of my method of guaranteeing
> identification of the model (model below; full replication code for a Poisson version is attached).
>
> For a 2-dimensional latent space model, I constrain the latent positions of the first three observations in the
> parameters{} block to lie in particular quadrants in R^2. In the model{} block, the latent positions of these
> observations also get their own priors before they are merged with the rest of the observations to form a n-by-2 matrix
> of latent positions (from which pairwise Euclidean distances are calculated).
>
> Is this the proper/efficient way to go about constraining particular elements of a matrix in Stan?

It's efficient. I wish it were more elegant, but I don't know
a better way to do it.

The other way to do it is to do the transforms yourself. But then
you have to fuss with Jacobians if you're using the elements on
the left-hand side.

If you constrain parameters to intervals as you did, you should make
sure they're wide enough to cover any reasonable posterior value.
At that point, you have a proper uniform distribution on the parameters,
so you don't need to add normal priors unless you believe their
shape is reasonable (that is, that those [0,5] constrained params
are more likely to be 2.5 than other values).

> Beyond fixing the
> observations' positions (my solution in a previous maximum likelihood version), any other ideas on how I can help
> guarantee identification? I am new to Bayesian modeling and Stan, so any suggestions would be welcomed.

What non-identifiabilities do you have? It looks from the
model that it's just an offset identity due to this line:
> D[idx] <- sqrt(dot_self(pos[i] - pos[j]));

So you probably have to pin down values for pos[] more than you have.
You can fix one value to a hard constraint.

Or you can add in an intercept and give pos stronger centering priors.

How do you choose the value(s) to fix?

Gelman and Hill have a nice discussion in their Regression book which we need
to repeat in Stan terms in our manual.

Also, you can replace this:
y ~ poisson(exp(beta - D));

with

y ~ poisson_log(beta - D);

It should be better-behaved arithmetically and faster. (The _log
is the Poisson with a log-transformed parameter, so that

poission_log(u) =def= poisson(exp(u))

- Bob

> ~Jason

parts: Dear Bob,

On Sunday, September 8, 2013 8:37:15 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:

It's efficient.  I wish it were more elegant, but I don't know
a better way to do it.
Thanks. Glad I was on the right track, despite the inelegance.

If you constrain parameters to intervals as you did, you should make 
sure they're wide enough to cover any reasonable posterior value.
At that point, you have a proper uniform distribution on the parameters,
so you don't need to add normal priors unless you believe their
shape is reasonable (that is, that those [0,5] constrained params
are more likely to be 2.5 than other values).

For actual data, I will have to play with the prior (and will start with a uniform). For my simulations, I wanted something that would estimate quickly. Is there a clear way to tell if the constraints aren't wide enough?

What non-identifiabilities do you have?  It looks from the
model that it's just an offset identity due to this line:

 >              D[idx] <- sqrt(dot_self(pos[i] - pos[j]));

So you probably have to pin down values for pos[] more than you have.
You can fix one value to a hard constraint.

Or you can add in an intercept and give pos stronger centering priors.

How do you choose the value(s) to fix?

The response is a function of the pairwise distances (the D vector in the model), which are invariant to translation, rotation, and reflection, but the latent positions are not. In my substantive applications, I have a good idea about where some of the observations should be placed in the latent space; e.g., I know (or can argue) that particular politicians are to the right or left of others. I could simply fix the positions of a couple actors, but in some of my applications I would like to allow a little more flexibility, since the positions are more debatable (this is something of a "cosmetic issue", since the relative distances shouldn't be affected). Of course, in testing the model, setting particular observations is arbitrary -- I'm just doing it to make sure the model is doing what I think it should.

Another option I have thought about is just to deal with the non-invariance of the latent positions through post-processing; i.e., some form of multidimensional scaling. This is what HRH do in the original paper -- they perform a Procrustes transformation with the pairwise geodesic distances as the reference distance matrix. This appears to work for their applications but seems to me to be a bit ad hoc and may not translate well to a broader set of problems where the latent positions are substantively meaningful. I could also just do the MDS by using particular observations as a reference, but that doesn't get around the issue of having to pick fixed locations for those observations. Another reason to have the observations constrained in the model, as I currently do, is that it allows me to run and compare multiple chains. 

Sorry, that's probably more info that you wanted, but it's my current thinking on the issue.

Gelman and Hill have a nice discussion in their Regression book which we need
to repeat in Stan terms in our manual.

Also, you can replace this:

   y ~ poisson(exp(beta - D));

with

   y ~ poisson_log(beta - D);

It should be better-behaved arithmetically and faster.  (The _log
is the Poisson with a log-transformed parameter, so that

    poission_log(u) =def= poisson(exp(u))

That's good to know. Thank you for your reply.

~Jason

- Bob

I'd be very interested to see what happens with a post-transform.
And we're always happy to help with concrete fitting issues when
